name: Practical Nutrition
goal: Broad literacy across nutrition science — foundations, metabolism, dietary patterns, supplements, and public health policy — with the ability to read primary evidence and evaluate claims independently
notes: Evidence appraisal is deliberately the depth-0 root: nutrition's polarization is primarily a reading problem, so the graph teaches GRADE, effect sizes, risk of bias, and conflicts of interest before content. All artifacts are drawn from verified source material in sources/practical_nutrition/ — see MANIFEST.md. Two concepts are flagged source-thin: energy_availability and population_vs_individual.

concepts.name: Study Designs and the Evidence Hierarchy

practical_artifacts.label: Eligibility criteria from CD013617 (HIIT) — what the design excludes
practical_artifacts.value: We included randomised control trials (RCTs) that compared HIIT with a non-exercise control (comparison 1) or with MICT (comparison 2) over four weeks or longer in healthy adults (aged 18-64 years) who were sedentary at baseline. We excluded studies of athletes, as we were interested in the benefits of HIIT for public health, not for performance.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Eligibility criteria define who the answer applies to. This review cannot tell you anything about athletes.

practical_artifacts.label: Design mix in CD014794 (school feeding) — not RCT-only
practical_artifacts.value: We included individually randomized, cluster-randomized, and cross-over trials, as well as longitudinal non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSIs).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Including NRSIs broadens the evidence but weakens causal claims. Ask what designs a review admitted before trusting its conclusion.

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN position statement on fat loss and lean mass accrual
practical_artifacts.value:
3) Diets primarily focused on fat loss are driven by a sustained caloric deficit. The higher the baseline body fat level, the more aggressively the caloric deficit may be imposed. Slower rates of weight loss can better preserve lean mass (LM) in leaner subjects.
4) Diets focused primarily on accruing LM are driven by a sustained caloric surplus to facilitate anabolic processes and support increasing resistance-training demands.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Deficit magnitude is conditional on starting body fat — not a fixed number.

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN on adaptive thermogenesis
practical_artifacts.value: 8) The long-term success of a diet depends upon compliance and suppression or circumvention of mitigating factors such as adaptive thermogenesis.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Energy out is not a constant; it responds to intake.

practical_artifacts.label: CD013617 (HIIT) — two certainty levels for two outcomes in ONE review
practical_artifacts.value:
HIIT compared with a non-exercise control ... reduces waist circumference (MD -3.56 cm, 95% CI -6.14 to -0.98; 8 studies, 270 participants; high-certainty evidence).

The evidence for the effect of HIIT on systolic blood pressure is very uncertain (MD -5.22 mmHg, 95% CI -12.27 to 1.84; 7 studies, 215 participants; very low-certainty evidence).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Certainty is assigned per outcome, not per study. The same review is simultaneously high and very-low certainty.

practical_artifacts.label: CD015988 — what a collapsed evidence base looks like
practical_artifacts.value:
All 16 reported outcomes rated very low-certainty. Example: BMI (mean difference -1.52 kg/m2, 95% CI -2.74 to -0.29; I2 = 0%; 2 studies, 118 children; very low-certainty evidence).

Authors' conclusions: 'Serious methodological limitations, clinical heterogeneity, small-study effects, and imprecise results constrained this evidence base. Future high-quality and better-reported RCTs will likely change our findings.'
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: A statistically significant result (CI excludes zero) can still be very low certainty. Significance and certainty are different questions.

practical_artifacts.label: CD003177 (omega-3) — the strongest profile in this source set
practical_artifacts.value: 5 high-certainty outcomes, 7 moderate, 8 low. Authors' conclusions: 'This is the most extensive systematic assessment of effects of omega-3 fats on cardiovascular health to date. Moderate- and low-certainty evidence suggests that increasing LCn3 slightly reduces risk of coronary heart disease mortality and events, and reduces serum triglycerides.'
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Note 'slightly' paired with high certainty — confident knowledge of a small effect.

concepts.name: Effect Sizes, Confidence Intervals, and Heterogeneity

practical_artifacts.label: CD015092 (semaglutide) — MD and RR side by side
practical_artifacts.value: Semaglutide reduces percentage body weight (mean difference (MD) -10.73, 95% CI -12.24 to -9.21; 15 studies, 8651 participants; high-certainty evidence) and increases the proportion of people achieving 5% weight loss (risk ratio (RR) 2.68, 95% CI 2.30 to 3.12; 12 studies, 7458 participants; high-certainty evidence).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: MD is on the outcome's own scale; RR is a ratio of probabilities. They answer different questions about the same drug.

practical_artifacts.label: CD015092 — severe heterogeneity in the long-term result
practical_artifacts.value: At long-term follow-up, semaglutide likely reduces percentage body weight (MD -11.11, 95% CI -16.47 to -5.75; I2 = 94%; 2 studies, 15,124 participants; moderate-certainty evidence).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: I2 = 94% means the two studies disagree badly. A pooled estimate from wildly heterogeneous studies is a weak summary even with 15,124 participants.

practical_artifacts.label: CD015988 — a CI that crosses no-effect
practical_artifacts.value:
body weight (MD -0.86 kg, 95% CI -3.17 to 1.46; I2 = 0%; 2 studies, 118 children; very low-certainty evidence)
serious adverse events (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.10 to 11.76; 1 study, 222 children; very low-certainty evidence)
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: The RR interval spans 0.10 to 11.76 — a hundredfold range. That is not evidence of no harm; it is no usable evidence either way.

concepts.name: EAR, RDA, AI, UL, AMDR, and CDRR

practical_artifacts.label: DRI EARs, males 19-30 y (Appendix J, DRI Sodium & Potassium 2019)
practical_artifacts.value:
Calcium      800 mg/d
Carbohydrate 100 g/d
Protein     0.66 g/kg/d
Vitamin A    625 ug/d
Vitamin C     75 mg/d
Vitamin D     10 ug/d
Vitamin E     12 mg/d
Thiamin      1.0 mg/d
Riboflavin   1.1 mg/d
Niacin        12 mg/d
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: An EAR meets the needs of only half the population. It is a population planning tool, not a personal target.

practical_artifacts.label: The EAR footnote — which nutrients have no EAR
practical_artifacts.value: NOTES: An Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirements of half of the healthy individuals in a group. EARs have not been established for vitamin K, pantothenic acid, biotin, choline, chromium, fluoride, manganese, potassium, sodium, chloride, or other nutrients not yet evaluated via the DRI process.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: When there is no EAR there is no RDA either — those nutrients get an AI instead, which is a weaker construct.

practical_artifacts.label: The six DRI constructs present in Appendix J
practical_artifacts.value:
EAR   Estimated Average Requirement   meets 50% of a group
RDA   Recommended Dietary Allowance   meets 97-98% of a group
AI    Adequate Intake                 used when evidence is too thin for an EAR
UL    Tolerable Upper Intake Level     above this, risk rises
AMDR  Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range
CDRR  Chronic Disease Risk Reduction Intake  (new in 2019)
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: CDRR is the 2019 innovation — an intake target based on chronic disease risk rather than deficiency.

concepts.name: Protein, Amino Acids, and Protein Quality

practical_artifacts.label: FDC protein and nitrogen columns
practical_artifacts.value:
1002  Nitrogen   G
1003  Protein    G
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Protein is usually derived from measured nitrogen via a conversion factor — see food_protein_conversion_factor.csv (366 rows). The factor differs by food.

practical_artifacts.label: FDC carbohydrate fraction columns
practical_artifacts.value:
1005  Carbohydrate, by difference   G
1009  Starch                        G
1010  Sucrose                       G
1006  Fiber, crude (DO NOT USE - Archived)  G
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: 'By difference' means total mass minus water, protein, fat and ash. Errors in any of those propagate into the carbohydrate figure.

practical_artifacts.label: WHO on where saturated fat is found
practical_artifacts.value: Saturated fatty acids can be found in fatty meat, dairy foods, and hard fats and oils such as butter, ghee, lard, palm oil and coconut oil.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Palm and coconut oil are plant fats that are predominantly saturated. 'Plant-based' does not imply unsaturated.

concepts.name: Vitamins and Minerals: Classes and Units

practical_artifacts.label: Equivalence units — the footnotes that change the number
practical_artifacts.value:
Niacin:     1 mg NE = 60 mg tryptophan
Folate:     1 DFE = 1 ug food folate = 0.6 ug folic acid from fortified food
                  = 0.5 ug of a supplement taken alone
Vitamin A:  1 RAE = 1 ug retinol = 12 ug beta-carotene = 24 ug alpha-carotene
Vitamin E:  counts only RRR- and the 2R-stereoisomeric forms of alpha-tocopherol,
            not the 2S- forms found in fortified foods and supplements
practical_artifacts.source_note: Footnotes, FDA RDI table (2016-11867) and DRI Appendix J
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Folic acid from a supplement is ~2x as bioavailable as food folate. The unit encodes the bioavailability difference.

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN position statement, point 2
practical_artifacts.value: 2) All body composition assessment methods have strengths and limitations.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Deliberately terse in the source. The teaching work is unpacking which limitation matters for which decision.

practical_artifacts.label: Outcome measures used across the Cochrane obesity reviews
practical_artifacts.value:
BMI (kg/m2) | BMI z-score | body weight (kg) | body fat percentage |
waist circumference (cm) | waist-to-hip ratio | adiposity and fat distribution
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: CD013617 found high-certainty benefit on waist circumference but no clear effect on waist-to-hip ratio. Which proxy you pick changes the answer.

practical_artifacts.label: Join pattern for nutrient-per-100-kcal in FDC
practical_artifacts.value:
food.csv          (fdc_id, description, data_type)
  |- food_nutrient.csv  (fdc_id, nutrient_id, amount)
       |- nutrient.csv    (id, name, unit_name)

Filter: data_type == 'foundation_food'
Energy: nutrient_id 1008 (kcal per 100 g)
Then:   amount_per_100kcal = amount * 100 / energy_kcal
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: FDC amounts are per 100 g of edible portion. Converting to per-calorie requires the energy row for the same fdc_id.

practical_artifacts.label: FDC portion tables
practical_artifacts.value:
food_portion.csv   10,951 rows   maps a household measure to gram weight per fdc_id
measure_unit.csv      123 rows   unit vocabulary (cup, tbsp, piece, ...)
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Gram weight per 'cup' is food-specific and lives in food_portion.csv, not in a generic conversion table.

concepts.name: Risk of Bias: RoB 1 and RoB 2

practical_artifacts.label: Two different tools across two reviews
practical_artifacts.value:
CD015988: 'Pairs of review authors independently assessed the risk of bias in included studies using the original version of the Cochrane tool (RoB 1).'

CD013617: 'We used the Cochrane risk of bias tool (RoB 2) to assess the risk of bias in the RCTs.'
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: RoB 1 is domain-judgement per study; RoB 2 is per-result and more structured. Reviews from the same year can use either.

practical_artifacts.label: CD013617 — the specific reasons certainty was downgraded
practical_artifacts.value: The certainty of the evidence was downgraded for inconsistency, imprecision, and risk of bias (mainly due to lack of detail on randomisation and no available protocol or trial registration).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: 'No available protocol or trial registration' is a bias signal you can check yourself on any paper.

practical_artifacts.label: CD013617 — an absence that is not a reassurance
practical_artifacts.value: No studies reported all-cause mortality or adverse events. ... There were no reports of adverse events, and we are unsure if the studies actively monitored for them.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Unreported is not the same as did-not-occur. The review authors flag their own uncertainty about whether anyone looked.

concepts.name: Funding Sources and Conflicts of Interest

practical_artifacts.label: CD015092 (semaglutide) — industry involvement stated in the abstract
practical_artifacts.value:
We included 18 RCTs (27,949 participants) ... Seventeen RCTs reported that the drug manufacturer had a major role in their design, conduct, analysis, or writing.

Authors' conclusions: 'Most studies were funded by the drug's manufacturer, raising important concerns about conflicts of interest.'
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: This coexists with high-certainty evidence of weight loss. A conflict of interest is a reason for scrutiny, not automatic dismissal.

practical_artifacts.label: The same pattern across all three GLP-1 reviews
practical_artifacts.value:
CD015092 semaglutide:  17 of 18 RCTs, manufacturer had a major role
CD016018 tirzepatide:  'All the included studies were funded by the drug manufacturer'
CD016017 liraglutide:  'The drug manufacturer funded 22 studies'
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Independent evidence on this entire drug class is nearly absent. That is a structural feature of the field, not a quirk of one review.

practical_artifacts.label: Non-industry funding, for contrast
practical_artifacts.value:
CD015988: 'The Department of Nutrition and Food Safety at the World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned and provided financial support for this work.'
CD015092: 'This Cochrane review was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO).'
CD013617: 'funded (in part) by the National Institute of Health Research (NIHR) and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO).'
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Distinguish who funded the review from who funded the underlying trials. CD015092 is a WHO-funded review of industry-funded trials.

concepts.name: Null Results vs. Absence of Evidence

practical_artifacts.label: CD015610 (intermittent fasting) — a genuine null
practical_artifacts.value: Compared to regular dietary advice, intermittent fasting may result in little to no difference in weight loss or quality of life. ... These approaches did not differ in achieving weight loss, producing no clinically meaningful changes in most of the outcomes considered in this review.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Trials were done, outcomes were measured, and the answer was 'no meaningful difference'. That is a finding.

practical_artifacts.label: CD013501 (vegan) — absence of evidence, not a null
practical_artifacts.value: Studies were generally small with few participants contributing to each comparison group. None of the included studies report on CVD clinical events. There is currently insufficient information to draw conclusions about the effects of vegan dietary interventions on CVD risk factors.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Nobody measured the outcome. This says nothing about whether vegan diets work — contrast sharply with the IF null above.

practical_artifacts.label: CD013729 (DASH) — a third category: inconclusive on hard outcomes only
practical_artifacts.value: The effect of the DASH diet on major cardiovascular outcomes - including myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality - remains inconclusive due to a lack of robust long-term evidence. ... While the DASH diet may reduce blood pressure, total cholesterol, and triglyceride levels while increasing HDL cholesterol ... it appears to have little to no effect on LDL cholesterol.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Three distinct states in three reviews: measured-and-null, never-measured, and measured-for-surrogates-but-not-endpoints.

practical_artifacts.label: Four protein numbers from three authorities
practical_artifacts.value:
DRI EAR, adult:              0.66 g/kg/d   (meets 50% of the group)
FDA DRV, food label:           50 g/d      (2,000 kcal reference, ages 4+)
ISSN, lean-mass retention
  in a deficit:              2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM
ISSN, 'very high' intake:       >3 g/kg
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: A ~5x spread. Each number is correct for its own question: population adequacy, label reference, or athletic lean-mass retention.

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN body composition stand, point 6
practical_artifacts.value: 6) Increasing dietary protein to levels significantly beyond current recommendations may result in improved body composition. Higher protein intakes (2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM) may be required to maximize muscle retention in lean, resistance-trained subjects under hypocaloric conditions. Emerging research on very high protein intakes (>3 g/kg) has demonstrated that the known thermic, satiating, and LM-preserving effects of dietary protein might be amplified in resistance-training subjects.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Note the units: g/kg FFM, not g/kg bodyweight. Applying it to total bodyweight gives the wrong target.

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN nutrient timing, points 6-7
practical_artifacts.value:
6. Meeting the total daily intake of protein, preferably with evenly spaced protein feedings (approximately every 3 h during the day), should be viewed as a primary area of emphasis for exercising individuals.
7. Ingestion of essential amino acids (EAA; approximately 10 g) either in free form or as part of a protein bolus of approximately 20-40 g has been shown to maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis (MPS).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Total daily intake comes first; distribution is the refinement. The order in the source matters.

practical_artifacts.label: WHO carbohydrate guideline, headline recommendations
practical_artifacts.value:
Carbohydrate intake should come primarily from whole grains, vegetables,
  fruits and pulses (everyone aged 2+)
Adults: at least 400 g/d of vegetables and fruits
Adults: at least 25 g/d of naturally occurring dietary fibre

FDA DRV for Dietary Fiber (label reference): 28 g
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: WHO says 'naturally occurring' fibre — which excludes isolated fibres added to processed foods. The label DRV makes no such distinction.

practical_artifacts.label: Two different sugar constructs
practical_artifacts.value:
WHO 'free sugars'   — added sugars plus sugars naturally present in
                       honey, syrups, and fruit juices
FDA 'added sugars'  — DRV 50 g/d on a 2,000 kcal basis

Neither counts sugars intrinsic to whole fruit and vegetables or milk.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Fruit juice counts as free sugar for WHO. The two definitions do not overlap exactly, so the same food can score differently.

practical_artifacts.label: WHO on non-sugar sweeteners
practical_artifacts.value: WHO's existing guidance limits free sugars intake, and reducing consumption of free sugars should be accomplished without the use of non-sugar sweeteners.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: The recommendation is to reduce sweetness intake, not to substitute the sweetener.

practical_artifacts.label: Label reference vs. guideline target
practical_artifacts.value:
FDA DRV, saturated fat:  20 g/d  (2,000 kcal basis = 9% of energy)
FDA DRV, total fat:      78 g/d
WHO guideline:           the SFA and TFA guideline is GRADE-based and must be
                         read alongside WHO guidance on total fat, PUFA,
                         sugars, sodium, potassium and carbohydrate
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Compute it: 20 g x 9 kcal / 2,000 = 9% of energy. The label DRV already encodes a percent-of-energy target.

practical_artifacts.label: DGA 2025-2030 is contested on exactly this nutrient
practical_artifacts.value: Independent critiques of the 2025-2030 DGA (CSPI; Harvard Nutrition Source, Jan 2026) identify saturated fat contradictions among their objections.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: A live example of guideline-vs-evidence divergence. Read the guideline and its critiques together.

practical_artifacts.label: CD003177.PUB5 — inclusion criteria and conclusions
practical_artifacts.value:
We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that lasted at least 12 months and compared supplementation or advice to increase LCn3 or ALA intake, or both, versus usual care.

Authors' conclusions: 'This is the most extensive systematic assessment of effects of omega-3 fats on cardiovascular health to date. Moderate- and low-certainty evidence suggests that increasing LCn3 slightly reduces risk of coronary heart disease mortality and events, and reduces serum triglycerides (evidence mainly from supplement trials). Increasing ALA slightly reduces risk of cardiovascular events and arrhythmia.'

Certainty profile: 5 high, 7 moderate, 8 low, 0 very low.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: LCn3 (marine EPA/DHA) and ALA (plant) are assessed separately and behave differently. 'Omega-3' as a single category obscures this.

practical_artifacts.label: Sodium and potassium across the reference systems
practical_artifacts.value:
Sodium
  FDA DRV (label):     2,300 mg/d
  FDA RDI chloride:    2,300 mg/d
  DRI:                 no EAR established; has a CDRR (new in 2019)

Potassium
  FDA RDI (label):     4,700 mg/d
  DRI:                 no EAR established; AI only
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Neither has an EAR. Their targets come from chronic-disease risk (CDRR) rather than from a measured requirement.

practical_artifacts.label: Adequacy check workflow against real data
practical_artifacts.value:
1. Target:   DRI RDA (or AI) for the nutrient, life-stage group
2. Food:     food.csv -> fdc_id for a Foundation food
3. Content:  food_nutrient.csv where fdc_id matches, nutrient_id = target
4. Portion:  food_portion.csv -> gram weight for a realistic serving
5. Scale:    amount is per 100 g; multiply by portion_g / 100
6. Compare:  scaled amount vs RDA
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Step 5 is where most errors happen. FDC amounts are per 100 g of edible portion, not per serving.

practical_artifacts.label: Appendix J includes two UL tables
practical_artifacts.value:
Tolerable Upper Intake Levels, Vitamins
Tolerable Upper Intake Levels, Elements
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Not every nutrient has a UL. Absence of a UL means insufficient data to set one — not that unlimited intake is safe.

practical_artifacts.label: Where the UL gap bites — nutrients with no EAR
practical_artifacts.value:
No EAR established for: vitamin K, pantothenic acid, biotin, choline,
chromium, fluoride, manganese, potassium, sodium, chloride
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: These are exactly the nutrients where supplement dosing has the weakest scientific floor and ceiling.

concepts.name: Energy Availability and Low Energy Availability
concepts.source_status: THIN — no primary source on energy availability or RED-S. The AND/DC/ACSM 2016 joint position stand (Nutrition and Athletic Performance) is the needed reference and is paywalled. Teach only what issn_body_composition_2017 supports; flag the boundary to the learner rather than extrapolating.

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN body composition stand, point 9 — the acknowledged gap
practical_artifacts.value: 9) There is a paucity of research on women and older populations, as well as a wide range of untapped permutations of feeding frequency and macronutrient distribution at various energetic balances combined with training.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: The source names its own limits. Energy availability in female athletes sits inside this gap.

concepts.name: Deficit Magnitude and Lean Mass Preservation

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN points 3 and 8 — rate, baseline, and compliance
practical_artifacts.value:
3) Diets primarily focused on fat loss are driven by a sustained caloric deficit. The higher the baseline body fat level, the more aggressively the caloric deficit may be imposed. Slower rates of weight loss can better preserve lean mass (LM) in leaner subjects.

8) The long-term success of a diet depends upon compliance and suppression or circumvention of mitigating factors such as adaptive thermogenesis.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Two competing objectives: speed of fat loss vs. retention of lean mass. Leanness shifts the optimum toward slower.

concepts.name: Low-Carb, Ketogenic, High-Protein, and Intermittent Fasting

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN points 1, 5 and 7 — the equivalence claim
practical_artifacts.value:
1) There is a multitude of diet types and eating styles, whereby numerous subtypes fall under each major dietary archetype.

5) A wide range of dietary approaches (low-fat to low-carbohydrate/ketogenic, and all points between) can be similarly effective for improving body composition.

7) The collective body of intermittent caloric restriction research demonstrates no significant advantage over daily caloric restriction for improving body composition.

Archetypes assessed: very-low- and low-energy diets (VLED, LED), low-fat diets (LFD), low-carbohydrate diets (LCD), ketogenic diets (KD), high-protein diets (HPD), and intermittent fasting (IF).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Two independent sources reach the same verdict on IF — ISSN 2017 and Cochrane CD015610 (2026). Convergence across method and decade.

practical_artifacts.label: CD015610 — the Cochrane version of the same finding
practical_artifacts.value:
We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs that compared intermittent fasting (including time-restricted feeding, periodic fasting, alternate-day fasting) ...

Compared to regular dietary advice, intermittent fasting may result in little to no difference in weight loss or quality of life.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Note the subtypes bundled under 'intermittent fasting'. A null on the bundle is not a null on each subtype.

practical_artifacts.label: Four reviews, one outcome framework — side by side
practical_artifacts.value:
CD009825.PUB3  Mediterranean  2019  30 RCTs (22 primary, 8 secondary)
  Moderate-quality evidence for stroke reduction in primary prevention;
  low-quality for total and CVD mortality in secondary prevention.
  'There is still some uncertainty regarding the effects ... on clinical endpoints.'

CD013729.PUB2  DASH           2025
  Hard CV outcomes inconclusive; no trials on heart failure or revascularisation.
  Reduces BP, total cholesterol, triglycerides; raises HDL; little/no effect on LDL.

CD013501.PUB2  Vegan          2021
  'None of the included studies report on CVD clinical events.'
  Insufficient information to draw conclusions. 8 ongoing studies.

CD003177.PUB5  Omega-3        2020  5 high-certainty outcomes
  LCn3 slightly reduces CHD mortality and events; ALA slightly reduces CV events.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Same question, same method, four different epistemic states. The most-recommended patterns are not the best-evidenced ones.

practical_artifacts.label: CD009825 — pre-standardisation GRADE wording
practical_artifacts.value: The quality of evidence for the modest benefits on CVD risk factors in primary prevention is low or moderate, with a small number of studies reporting minimal harms. There is a paucity of evidence for secondary prevention.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: This 2019 review says 'quality of evidence'; the 2025-2026 reviews say 'certainty of evidence'. Same GRADE construct, renamed.

practical_artifacts.label: ISSN nutrient timing, points 2-5 — the numbers
practical_artifacts.value:
2. Endogenous glycogen stores are maximized by following a high-carbohydrate diet (8-12 g of carbohydrate/kg/day); moreover, these stores are depleted most by high volume exercise.

3. If rapid restoration of glycogen is required (< 4 h of recovery time) then the following strategies should be considered:
   a) aggressive carbohydrate refeeding (1.2 g/kg/h) with a preference towards carbohydrate sources that have a high (> 70) glycemic index
   b) the addition of caffeine (3-8 mg/kg)
   c) combining carbohydrates (0.8 g/kg/h) with protein (0.2-0.4 g/kg/h)

4. Extended (> 60 min) bouts of high intensity (> 70% VO2max) exercise challenge fuel supply and fluid regulation, thus carbohydrate should be consumed at a rate of ~30-60 g of carbohydrate/h in a 6-8% carbohydrate-electrolyte solution (6-12 fluid ounces) every 10-15 min throughout the entire exercise bout, particularly in those exercise bouts that span beyond 70 min.

5. Carbohydrate ingestion throughout resistance exercise (e.g., 3-6 sets of 8-12 repetition maximum [RM] using multiple exercises targeting all major muscle groups) has been shown to promote euglycemia and higher glycogen stores.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Every recommendation is gated on a threshold: >60 min, >70% VO2max, <4 h recovery. Below those thresholds the guidance does not apply.

practical_artifacts.label: CD003177 — what a well-evidenced supplement claim looks like
practical_artifacts.value: Moderate- and low-certainty evidence suggests that increasing LCn3 slightly reduces risk of coronary heart disease mortality and events, and reduces serum triglycerides (evidence mainly from supplement trials).
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: 'Slightly' is doing real work. A well-evidenced small effect is often marketed as a large one.

practical_artifacts.label: The three-number check on any supplement label
practical_artifacts.value:
1. Dose on the label
2. FDA RDI for that nutrient (the %DV denominator)
3. DRI Tolerable Upper Intake Level

If (1) greatly exceeds (2), ask why. If (1) approaches or exceeds (3), that is a
safety question, not a potency feature.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: A %DV over 100% is not automatically a problem, but it is automatically a question.

practical_artifacts.label: CD015092 (semaglutide) — the full outcome picture
practical_artifacts.value:
Medium term (6-17 months), vs placebo:
  percentage body weight   MD -10.73 (95% CI -12.24 to -9.21); 15 studies, 8651 pts; HIGH
  >=5% weight loss         RR 2.68 (95% CI 2.30 to 3.12); 12 studies, 7458 pts; HIGH
  non-serious AEs          RR 1.11 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.22); 13 studies, 8443 pts; LOW
  AEs leading to withdrawal RR 1.84 (95% CI 1.53 to 2.21); 15 studies, 9054 pts; MODERATE
  serious AEs              RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.29); 15 studies, 9054 pts; VERY LOW
  quality of life (SF-36 PF) MD 2.12 (95% CI 0.95 to 3.28); 9 studies, 6083 pts; MODERATE
  MACE                     RR 0.63 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.90); 9 studies, 7647 pts; LOW
  mortality                RR 0.69 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.98); 14 studies, 8953 pts; LOW

17 of 18 RCTs: manufacturer had a major role in design, conduct, analysis or writing.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Weight loss is high-certainty. Everything patients actually care about downstream — mortality, MACE, quality of life, serious harms — is low or very low.

practical_artifacts.label: The three drugs compared on certainty, not just efficacy
practical_artifacts.value:
CD015092 semaglutide  2 high / 9 moderate / 3 low / 2 very low   17 of 18 industry
CD016018 tirzepatide  0 high / 8 moderate / 6 low / 2 very low   all industry
CD016017 liraglutide  0 high / 5 moderate / 5 low / 8 very low   22 industry-funded
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Liraglutide has eight very-low-certainty outcomes. Ranking these drugs by headline weight loss ignores how differently well they are studied.

practical_artifacts.label: CD007654 — the older drug class, for contrast
practical_artifacts.value:
Our critical outcomes of death and cardiovascular complications were not the focus of the trials included in this review but were sometimes presented as part of an 'adverse events' outcome, with the resultant data providing only very low certainty evidence. Overall, the evidence for people with hypertension remains insufficient to draw conclusions.

'Several pharmaceutical products have been removed from the market due to safety concerns, whilst new drugs have been introduced.'
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Drugs in this class have been withdrawn before. Absence of long-term safety data is the historically relevant risk.

practical_artifacts.label: CD013617 — HIIT vs nothing, and HIIT vs moderate training
practical_artifacts.value:
58 RCTs, 2075 participants (14 to 90 per study), 4 to 16 weeks.

vs non-exercise control:
  VO2max              MD +5.98 mL/min/kg (95% CI 4.66 to 7.30); 16 studies, 517 pts; MODERATE
  waist circumference MD -3.56 cm (95% CI -6.14 to -0.98); 8 studies, 270 pts; HIGH
  waist-to-hip ratio  MD -0.01 (95% CI -0.03 to 0.01); 6 studies, 224 pts; MODERATE
  triglycerides       SMD -0.22 (95% CI -0.62 to 0.17); 9 studies, 262 pts; LOW
  systolic BP         MD -5.22 mmHg (95% CI -12.27 to 1.84); 7 studies, 215 pts; VERY LOW

vs moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT):
  VO2max              MD +1.39 mL/min/kg (95% CI 0.44 to 2.34); 37 studies, 1115 pts; LOW
  waist circumference MD +0.06 cm (95% CI -1.49 to 1.62); 15 studies, 407 pts; MODERATE
  systolic BP         MD -0.56 mmHg (95% CI -3.02 to 1.90); 18 studies, 515 pts; LOW

No studies reported all-cause mortality or adverse events.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Compare the two comparisons. Against nothing, HIIT looks strong; against moderate training, the advantage nearly vanishes. The comparator determines the story.

practical_artifacts.label: CD004366 — when new evidence does not move the estimate
practical_artifacts.value: Exercise may be moderately more effective than a control intervention for reducing symptoms of depression. Exercise appears to be no more or less effective than psychological or pharmacological treatments, though this conclusion is based on a few small trials. Long-term follow-up was rare. The addition of 35 RCTs (at least 2526 participants) to this update has had very little effect on the estimate of the benefit of exercise on symptoms of depression.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: 35 new RCTs, 2500+ participants, and the estimate barely moved. Stability under new data is itself evidence.

practical_artifacts.label: WHO Healthy diet fact sheet (2026-01-26) — the four core principles
practical_artifacts.value:
Healthy diets come in many forms, but the four core principles of adequacy, balance, moderation and diversity should be the foundation of any healthy diet.

A variety of minimally processed and unprocessed foods low in unhealthy fats, free sugars and sodium are the foundation of any healthy diet.

A diet must also be safe to be healthy, i.e. free from microbial and chemical contaminants.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: 'Healthy diets come in many forms' is a claim about the evidence — it matches CD009825/CD013729/CD013501 showing no single pattern with decisive superiority.

practical_artifacts.label: DGA 2025-2030 — a guideline and its critics
practical_artifacts.value:
Released 2026-01-07 by USDA and HHS; published at realfood.gov. Key message: 'Eat Real Food.'

Independent critiques published within days:
  CSPI, 'The Uncompromised Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030' (2026-01-07)
  Harvard Nutrition Source, 'Progress on added sugar, protein hype, saturated fat
    contradictions' (2026-01-09)
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Guidelines are policy documents shaped by process and constituency, not evidence syntheses. Read them as such, and read the critiques alongside.

practical_artifacts.label: Which authority governs which question
practical_artifacts.value:
What a US food label legally means    -> FDA (regulation, not evidence)
What a person requires               -> NASEM DRI (and EFSA, WHO)
What the evidence supports           -> Cochrane, GRADE-rated syntheses
What policy recommends               -> DGA, WHO guidelines

These can disagree without any of them being wrong.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Most nutrition arguments are two people citing different authorities for different question types.

concepts.name: Evaluating a Nutrition Claim End to End

practical_artifacts.label: The appraisal checklist, assembled from this graph
practical_artifacts.value:
1. What kind of claim is it — requirement, label, evidence, or policy?
2. Which authority actually governs that question?
3. Is there a systematic review? What is the per-outcome certainty?
4. Effect size and CI — does the interval cross no-effect? What is I2?
5. Which outcomes were measured, and which were never reported?
6. Who funded the trials, as distinct from who funded the review?
7. What was the comparator? (vs nothing, vs usual care, vs an active alternative)
8. Does the claim's population match the review's eligibility criteria?
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Steps 5 and 7 catch the most real-world claims. Most overstatement lives in an unreported outcome or a weak comparator.

practical_artifacts.label: Worked example — 'HIIT is better than steady cardio for heart health'
practical_artifacts.value:
Claim type: evidence claim -> Cochrane governs.
Review: CD013617.PUB2 (2026), 58 RCTs, 2075 participants.
Comparator matters: vs non-exercise, waist circumference -3.56 cm (HIGH certainty).
  vs MICT, waist circumference +0.06 cm, CI -1.49 to 1.62 (MODERATE) — no difference.
VO2max vs MICT: +1.39 mL/min/kg, LOW certainty.
Hard outcomes: no studies reported all-cause mortality. Adverse events unreported,
  and authors are 'unsure if the studies actively monitored for them'.
Population: sedentary adults 18-64. Athletes explicitly excluded.

Verdict: 'better than nothing' is well supported. 'Better than steady cardio' is a
slight VO2max edge at low certainty and no difference elsewhere. 'For heart health'
overreaches — nobody measured cardiac events.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: The claim is not false so much as three different claims, each with a different evidential standing.

concepts.name: Public Health Policy vs. Personal Decisions
concepts.source_status: THIN — CD014794 (school feeding) is the only population-level intervention review in the export. CD027633834/CD-equivalent sodium-policy review was considered and dropped. Teach the distinction conceptually; do not overclaim on policy effectiveness.

practical_artifacts.label: CD014794 — a population intervention judged on population outcomes
practical_artifacts.value:
In LMICs, school feeding programs lead to a slight improvement in math achievement, but may have little to no effect on reading achievement. School feeding programs lead to a slight increase in enrollment, but may have little to no impact on attendance. They likely lead to slight gains in HAZ and WAZ. There may be little to no association between school feeding and overweight/obesity, but the evidence is very uncertain.

Certainty profile: 2 high, 2 moderate, 2 low.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: The outcomes are enrollment and math scores — not nutrients. Population nutrition interventions get judged on population endpoints.

practical_artifacts.label: Same nutrient, two decision levels
practical_artifacts.value:
Sodium
  Individual:  DRI CDRR; FDA label DRV 2,300 mg/d; your own intake
  Population:  reformulation mandates, salt substitution, procurement standards

A 1 mmHg mean population BP reduction is a major public health win and
clinically irrelevant to any single person.
practical_artifacts.teaching_point: Effect sizes that are trivial individually can be decisive at population scale. This is the most common source of cross-talk in nutrition debates.
